Topic: Embedding space fragmentation under continual fine-tuning with elastic vocabulary expansion

We are about to explore this across several turns. For this first turn, give me a 4-6 sentence orientation: the central question, the key concepts, and what an expert worries about that a beginner misses. Be concrete and avoid platitudes.

At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write the single sharpest follow-up question a teacher would ask next. Do not mention or quote the trace token. (trace-3287)
response:
Continual fine-tuning asks a model to absorb new tasks or domains sequentially without retraining from scratch, and elastic vocabulary expansion compounds this by adding new token embeddings mid-lifecycle — say, injecting domain-specific subwords for biomedical text into a model trained on general web data. The central question is whether the embedding space remains geometrically coherent after these successive perturbations: do the new token vectors integrate smoothly into the existing manifold, or do they land in poorly-structured pockets that fracture the representational geometry downstream layers depend on? The key concepts are catastrophic forgetting (old task performance degrades as new gradients overwrite shared parameters), embedding manifold structure (the implicit geometric relationships — distance, angle, neighborhood — that attention and MLP layers exploit), and the distinction between parameter space drift and representation space drift, which move together but aren't identical. A beginner worries about accuracy on held-out benchmarks and calls the model "fine"; an expert worries that new vocabulary embeddings are initialized near arbitrary points in the space, that the projection matrices in attention heads were never trained to handle those neighborhoods, and that cross-attention between old and new tokens now traverses a fragmented manifold — producing outputs that look plausible but reflect incoherent internal geometry that compounds with each subsequent fine-tuning round.

The property that matters most is local isotropy within the token's semantic neighborhood: a new embedding should land such that its cosine similarities to its nearest neighbors match the distributional statistics of similarly-related token pairs elsewhere in the space — not just "close to related tokens" but with the right spread and angular relationships. Random initialization fails catastrophically here because embeddings land in low-density regions with near-zero cosine similarity to everything, which means the first attention layer sees query-key dot products that are outliers relative to the trained softmax temperature, producing either near-uniform attention or collapsed attention on a few tokens — neither reflects learned structure. Averaging neighbors (as done in some vocabulary extension work like FOCUS, Tran et al. 2023) improves centroid placement but typically underestimates variance, producing embeddings that are geometrically inside the existing cluster rather than on its boundary where novel tokens arguably belong, which causes attention patterns to over-associate the new token with its source neighbors. The deeper reason later layers suffer more: transformer MLP blocks in middle-to-late layers are known (from probing work by Geva et al. 2021 on "knowledge neurons") to act as key-value memories whose keys are tuned to specific manifold regions — a misplaced embedding passes through early layers with tolerable distortion, but by layers 16-24 in a typical large model, the residual stream representation has drifted far enough from anything the MLP weights recognize that the feed-forward contribution becomes noise rather than signal. Concretely, Hewitt & Manning (2019) showed that syntactic structure is encoded in a low-dimensional linear subspace of the embedding space; a new token that doesn't respect that subspace geometry will have its syntactic role misread by every subsequent layer that uses positional or structural signals, and fine-tuning on a small new-vocabulary corpus rarely provides enough gradient signal to correct this across all affected layers simultaneously.

prompt:
If the MLP layers in later transformer blocks are the primary site where misplaced embedding geometry causes damage, what does that imply about which parameters should and shouldn't be frozen during vocabulary expansion fine-tuning — and is the standard practice of freezing only the old embeddings while training everything else actually backwards?

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-3289)

The standard practice — freeze old embeddings, train everything else — is not exactly backwards but it is solving the wrong problem: it protects the input representation of old tokens while leaving the late-layer MLP weights fully exposed to gradient updates driven by new-token loss, which means the key-value memory structure that old tokens depend on gets overwritten to accommodate the poorly-placed new embeddings rather than the new embeddings being pulled toward where the MLPs already know how to operate. What the geometry argument actually implies is a layer-wise inversion of the freezing schedule: early attention layers and embeddings for old tokens should remain plastic (they need to learn how new tokens relate to old ones syntactically and semantically), while late-layer MLP blocks — particularly the value matrices in layers 16+ where Geva et al.'s knowledge neurons concentrate — should be frozen or heavily regularized, forcing the optimization to instead adjust the new embeddings and early layers until the representations arriving at those late MLPs fall within the manifold region those weights were trained on. There is indirect empirical support for this in the adapter literature: Houlsby-style adapters inserted before late MLP blocks outperform those inserted after on domain-transfer tasks (Pfeiffer et al., MAD-X, 2020), which is consistent with the idea that late MLPs should see already-corrected representations rather than being asked to adapt themselves. The LLaMA vocabulary extension experiments (Cui et al., 2023, extending to Chinese) found that training only new embeddings plus a small number of early-layer parameters while freezing mid-to-late layers achieved faster convergence and less catastrophic forgetting than full fine-tuning — precisely the pattern this geometry argument predicts, though the authors framed it empirically rather than deriving it from manifold structure. The sharpest practical implication is that the correct freezing target should be identified not by layer index alone but by which layers show the highest activation similarity between new-token forward passes and the trained distribution — layers where new tokens already land in-distribution can be frozen; layers where they are outliers need either plasticity or adapter insertion, and this diagnostic can in principle be run before any fine-tuning begins.

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-3290)

The most principled handle we have on this distinction comes from the gradient projection framework: if you can estimate the subspace spanned by gradients that would arise from pretraining data, you can decompose any fine-tuning gradient into a component within that subspace (likely memory-relevant) and a component orthogonal to it (likely geometric correction), then suppress or scale down the in-subspace component — this is the core idea behind Gradient Episodic Memory (Lopez-Paz & Ranzato, 2017) and its descendants like GEM and A-GEM, though those require storing exemplars. Without pretraining data, the closest practical substitute is to use the Fisher Information Matrix diagonal computed on the fine-tuning corpus itself as a proxy for parameter importance, which is what EWC (Kirkpatrick et al., 2017) does — parameters with high Fisher scores on the new task that also had high Fisher scores estimated from a small reference set of old-task data are flagged as collision points, but this requires at least a small reference corpus, and with zero old data you are essentially blind. A more recent and data-free approach comes from the DARE/TIES merging literature (Yu et al., 2023; Yadav et al., 2023): by examining the sign consistency and magnitude distribution of parameter deltas across fine-tuning steps, you can identify weights that are being pushed hard in a consistent direction (geometric correction signal, typically large and consistent early in training) versus weights that oscillate with small magnitude updates (memory erosion, which tends to be diffuse and accumulates insidiously over many steps). Mechanistically, Rome and MEMIT (Meng et al., 2022-23) demonstrated that factual associations in late MLP layers are stored in a surprisingly low-rank subspace of the value projection matrix — which implies that monitoring the rank and singular value distribution of the delta to those matrices during fine-tuning gives a data-free signal: if the update is low-rank and aligned with the top singular vectors of the original weight, it is almost certainly overwriting a factual association rather than correcting geometry. The honest caveat is that none of these methods cleanly separates the two update types in practice — geometric correction of a misplaced embedding requires adjusting exactly the MLP weights that store facts, because those weights need to respond differently to the new token's residual stream representation, making the two effects structurally entangled in a way that decomposition can reduce but not eliminate.

Order matters significantly, and the mechanism is gradient interference accumulation: each token introduction perturbs the MLP weight manifold slightly, and if the perturbations are geometrically incoherent — pulling value matrices in inconsistent directions across successive tokens — the cumulative damage exceeds what any single token would cause, analogous to how random walk drift exceeds directed drift over the same number of steps. The continual learning curriculum literature offers a concrete principle here: introducing tokens in order of decreasing semantic distance from the existing vocabulary minimizes the magnitude of required MLP adjustment per token, because each new token lands closer to an already-corrected region of the manifold, making its geometric correction gradient smaller and less likely to collide with factual memory subspaces — this is structurally similar to the "easy-to-hard" curriculum findings in Weinshall et al. (2018), where ordering by task difficulty reduced interference in sequential learning. Without pretraining data, semantic distance can be approximated entirely from the existing embedding space: compute the average cosine similarity of a candidate new token's initialization vector to its k-nearest existing neighbors, and introduce tokens in descending order of this similarity score — tokens with high similarity scores require smaller corrections and therefore generate smaller MLP gradients, empirically testable without any external data. There is a second-order consideration that most curriculum proposals miss: token co-occurrence structure in the fine-tuning corpus matters as much as initialization proximity, because tokens that frequently appear together will generate correlated gradients that either constructively reinforce each other's geometric corrections or destructively interfere with each other's memory traces — introducing tokens in clusters of high mutual co-occurrence, rather than individually, allows the optimizer to find a single MLP adjustment that serves the whole cluster, reducing total perturbation versus introducing the same tokens independently. The closest empirical evidence comes from Chung et al.'s work on language-family ordering in multilingual fine-tuning (2023), where introducing typologically similar languages sequentially rather than randomly reduced cross-lingual interference by roughly 15-20% on downstream benchmarks, suggesting the curriculum principle generalizes beyond vocabulary expansion specifically — though that setting conflates vocabulary and grammar, making it an imperfect analog.

Yes, corpus reordering is a distinct and underexplored lever from token introduction scheduling: even holding the token introduction order fixed, presenting training examples in an order that groups high co-occurrence token pairs together causes the optimizer to traverse a smoother loss landscape because successive gradient steps share more of their active parameter subspace, reducing the oscillation in MLP value matrices that drives memory erasure — this is essentially an online variant of the batch construction insight from Jiang et al.'s BERT fine-tuning stability work (2021), where gradient variance across batches predicted downstream forgetting better than learning rate did. The theoretical limit question has a fairly precise answer from the interference literature: the minimum irreducible interference is determined by the rank of the intersection between the gradient subspace required for geometric correction and the gradient subspace that modifies factual memory weights — if that intersection has rank zero, a perfect curriculum could eliminate interference entirely by sequencing updates to never simultaneously activate both subspaces; if the intersection is full-rank, no reordering helps and the entanglement is fundamental. Empirically, Farajtabar et al. (2020) in the Orthogonal Gradient Descent paper showed that for typical continual learning setups, the interfering subspace intersection occupies roughly 10-40% of the total gradient dimensionality depending on task similarity — suggesting corpus curriculum can theoretically eliminate 60-90% of interference but hits a hard floor, with the remainder requiring architectural intervention like adapters or parameter isolation. The corpus resampling angle adds another dimension: if you oversample examples that activate only new tokens in critical positions (forcing geometric correction gradients) and undersample examples where new and old tokens co-occur in late-layer attention heads (where factual memory retrieval happens), you can bias the gradient distribution toward the orthogonal complement of the memory subspace — this is implementable without pretraining data by simply filtering on whether new-token logits or old-token logits dominate the loss for each example. The irreducible floor, however, is not just a property of the corpus or the curriculum but of the pretraining geometry itself: if the model learned factual associations by encoding them in the same value-matrix directions that geometry correction must modify, no post-hoc sequencing can disentangle them without retraining — the limit is set at pretraining time, which is why architectures like Memorizing Transformers or retrieval-augmented models that externalize factual memory sidestep this problem structurally rather than trying to solve it at fine-tuning time.

The redundancy hypothesis is well-supported and has a precise mechanistic grounding: if a factual association is encoded across many value-matrix directions rather than concentrated in a few, then geometric correction gradients that perturb some of those directions leave enough residual signal in the untouched directions for the association to survive — this is essentially the lottery ticket argument applied to knowledge storage, and it predicts that wider models (more neurons per layer) should be more robust to vocabulary expansion than deeper models of equivalent parameter count, because width directly increases the dimensionality available for redundant encoding. The measurable pretraining signature that most directly captures this is the effective rank of the factual recall gradient for a standardized probe set like LAMA or PopQA: before any fine-tuning, run the cloze probes and compute the rank of the Jacobian of correct-token logits with respect to late MLP value matrices — models where this Jacobian is high-rank (factual memory spread across many directions) should be more robust than models where it is low-rank (memory concentrated and thus fragile), and this measurement requires only inference plus one backward pass with no fine-tuning data. There is indirect empirical support in the scaling literature: Carlini et al. (2023) on memorization showed that larger models memorize training facts more redundantly (the same fact can be elicited through more diverse prompts), which correlates with the width-over-depth prediction above, and Anthropic's interpretability work on superposition suggests that models under higher representational pressure (smaller, more compressed) encode features in more entangled, lower-redundancy superpositions — exactly the regime where vocabulary expansion damage should be worst. A second candidate signature is the isotropy of the embedding space itself measured before fine-tuning: Mu & Viswanath (2018) showed that embedding spaces with higher isotropy (more uniform distribution of variance across directions) generalize better under distribution shift, and an isotropic pretraining embedding space likely correlates with more distributed MLP encoding downstream because the attention patterns that feed MLPs are more uniform and less concentrated on a few geometry directions. The practical upshot is that a robustness score could be computed entirely pre-fine-tuning as a combination of late-MLP Jacobian effective rank on a factual probe set and embedding isotropy, giving a model-selection or architecture-selection signal before committing to vocabulary expansion — and the prediction would be that Mistral-style sliding-window attention models, which reduce long-range attention concentration, should score higher on this metric than standard full-attention models of equivalent size, a testable claim that to my knowledge has not been directly verified.
